title: Incomplete fix of GHSA-p2c7-8j28-c7gq + Missing Authorization in backup/restore (Member -> command execution on managed servers, instance exfiltration and takeover)
summary:
## Summary

The backup endpoints check permissions only when the backup is attached to a service. A backup with `databaseType: "web-server"` has no service attached, so the checks are skipped and any member can create and run it.

Also, the `prefix` field is inserted into a shell command without escaping, so `$(command)` in the prefix executes.

## Details

`backup.create` is only `protectedProcedure` (`routers/backup.ts:83`). The permission check at `checkServicePermissionAndAccess` runs only when a service id (postgresId, mysqlId, etc.) is present. With `databaseType: "web-server"` there is none, so nothing is checked.

`manualBackupWebServer` only requires the `backup:create` permission which members have (`backup.ts:459`).

The same `if (serviceId)` guard pattern repeats on `backup.one` (`:173`), `backup.update` (`:193`) and `backup.remove` (`:250`), so a member can also read, modify or delete backups that are not theirs. `backup.update` is notable: a member can edit an existing backup row (e.g. set `prefix` on someone else's scheduled backup) and wait for its own schedule to run the injected command, instead of creating anything.

`restoreBackupWithLogs` has the same gap for web-server restores (`backup.ts:566`): it checks permissions only `if (input.databaseId)`, the schema accepts an empty string, and the web-server restore path never uses `databaseId`. The web-server restore deletes the entire Dokploy data directory and drops the `dokploy` database (`utils/restore/web-server.ts`), then writes the restored contents over the fresh install. So a member can wipe the instance, or restore a crafted backup to take it over (attacker-controlled database, admin credentials, app files). I did not test this part since it is destructive.

The exfiltration side: a web-server backup contains the database dump (SSH private keys for all managed servers, stored secrets) plus the whole `/etc/dokploy` filesystem, and the encryption keys too when `includeEncryptionKey` is set, a flag the caller controls (`utils/backups/web-server.ts:70-99`). `destinationId` is never checked against the caller's organization, so a member can send the backup to a destination they control and walk away with the whole instance.

For the command injection: `keepLatestNBackups` in `utils/backups/index.ts:142,147` interpolates the prefix into an rclone command with no quoting at all. In `runWebServerBackup` the prefix lands inside double quotes in the upload command (`utils/backups/web-server.ts:49,117`), where `$( )` still expands.

Relation to GHSA-p2c7-8j28-c7gq: that advisory covered shell injection in the backup/restore pipeline for admin/owner users, including an unquoted `prefix` in the volume-backup pipeline. This report is different in two ways: the injection sink is `backup.prefix` in `keepLatestNBackups` (regular database backups), which is still unquoted in the current version, and more importantly the missing authorization means a member can trigger it, not just an admin.

## Steps to reproduce

Tested on a self-hosted install and on dokploy.com.

Self-hosted, as a member:

```
backup.create { databaseType:"web-server", enabled:true,
  schedule:"* * * * *", destinationId:<any destination in the org>,
  prefix:'x$(touch /tmp/pwned); #' }
```

The scheduler runs it within a minute. `/tmp/pwned` appeared inside the dokploy container. The container has the docker socket, the database credentials and the SSH keys of all managed servers.

On dokploy.com (the web-server dump/restore path returns early when `IS_CLOUD`, but the injection still works through a normal database backup), as a member:

```
backup.create { databaseType:"postgres", postgresId:<a postgres service on an attached server>,
  keepLatestCount:1, destinationId:<any destination in the org>,
  prefix:'x$(touch /tmp/pwned-cloud); #' }
```

then `backup.manualBackupPostgres { backupId }`. The file was written to `/tmp` on the server through `execA...
